purpose: Prevents attacks and breaches from going undetected by ensuring security-relevant events are logged, monitored, and alerted on in time to respond.
summary: Security Logging and Alerting Failures occur when an application doesn't log security-relevant events, logs them without sufficient detail, or has no effective alerting and monitoring in place, allowing attacks to go undetected long enough for attackers to achieve their goals and cover their tracks.
expectedStatementElements: What security-relevant events are logged (authentication attempts, access control failures, input validation failures, high-value transactions)
How logs are protected from tampering or deletion, and how long they're retained
What alerting exists for suspicious patterns, and how quickly those alerts reach someone who can respond
How the organization tests or validates that logging and alerting actually work as expected (e.g., through tabletop exercises or red-team activity)
evidenceExamples: Logging configuration showing which security-relevant events are captured and with what detail
Log integrity and retention configuration (write-once storage, retention period, access restrictions)
Alerting rules and escalation path for suspicious activity
Results from a tabletop exercise, red-team test, or incident simulation validating detection and response
commonGaps: Security-relevant events like failed logins or access control failures aren't logged at all, or lack enough detail to investigate
Logs can be modified or deleted by the same accounts being monitored, undermining their value as evidence
Alerts exist on paper but don't actually reach anyone in a timely way, or generate so much noise they're ignored
Logging and alerting have never been tested against a simulated attack to confirm they'd actually catch it
interviewQuestions: If someone tried repeatedly to log in as another user, would that show up anywhere, and would anyone see it in time?
Could an attacker who compromised an account also delete or alter the logs showing what they did?
When an alert fires, how long does it typically take before a person actually looks at it?
Has your logging and alerting setup ever been tested against a simulated attack to see if it actually works?
